readings.title: Uncle Benjamin, a hidden Bible and a stolen wharf
readings.challenge: Sort what Franklin remembers himself, what he was told, and what he only half recalls (“if I remember the words rightly”).
readings.focus: Family stories of conscience and ingenuity, told by a man looking for the roots of his own character.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. He began in 1771 with a letter to his son William, so “you” is William. His family came from Ecton in Northamptonshire, England. Queen Mary (reigned 1553–1558) persecuted Protestants; an apparitor was an officer of the church courts; conventicles were forbidden religious meetings of Protestants outside the Church of England. A joint-stool is a wooden stool; a tallow-chandler makes candles; the “tithe” of his sons is the one in ten given to the church; emmets are ants.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Ancestry and Early Youth in Boston, from his uncles John and Benjamin through the wharf of stolen stones; opens “John was bred a dyer, I believe of woollens, Benjamin was bred a silk dyer, serving an…”; closes “…usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest.”.

questions.prompt: What does Franklin tell us about his uncle Benjamin, and why might he dwell on this uncle in particular?
facilitatorNotes: Benjamin was a silk dyer who wrote occasional poems, invented his own shorthand, took down sermons and collected political pamphlets “from 1641 to 1717.” Franklin was named after him and, only lately, came upon his pamphlet collection in London with the uncle’s notes in the margins.

The uncle is a reader, writer and collector, like Franklin. The comment “too much, perhaps, for his station” shows Franklin’s awareness of rank: a tradesman taking a large interest in politics was unusual. Ask whether Franklin sees himself in that phrase.
evidence: I was named after this uncle, there being a particular affection between him and my father.
He was also much of a politician; too much, perhaps, for his station.

questions.prompt: Three stories in this passage are about religious freedom: the Bible under the stool, Josiah’s move to New England, and Peter Folger’s verses. What does each show, and what does Franklin admire?
facilitatorNotes: The family hid an English Bible under a stool, with a child watching for the apparitor; Josiah left England with others who “expected to enjoy their mode of religion with freedom”; Folger wrote for “liberty of conscience” for Baptists, Quakers and others. Franklin praises Folger’s “decent plainness and manly freedom.”
Notice that the stool story is secondhand (“This anecdote I had from my uncle Benjamin”) and Folger’s verse quoted from memory. Franklin is open about how he knows each story.
evidence: it was fastened open with tapes under and within the cover of a joint-stool
This anecdote I had from my uncle Benjamin.
The whole appeared to me as written with a good deal of decent plainness and manly freedom.

questions.prompt: Why did Franklin’s father take him out of the grammar school? What does the phrase “reasons that he gave to his friends in my hearing” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The cost of college for so large a family, and the “mean living” many educated men later earned. The boy overheard the reasons rather than being told them, and he records them along with his own success at the top of his class.
Some readers sense a lasting regret; others see Franklin simply reporting a sensible decision. He does not comment, which leaves the reader to weigh the loss.
evidence: from a view of the expense of a college education, which having so large a family he could not well afford
reasons that he gave to his friends in my hearing

questions.prompt: Franklin says the wharf story “shows an early projecting public spirit, tho' not then justly conducted.” What was public-spirited about it, and what was unjust? Does his father’s lesson settle the matter?
facilitatorNotes: The boys built something useful for all of them, working together “like so many emmets”; but the stones belonged to someone else’s house. Franklin argued for usefulness, and his father “convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest.”
The adult Franklin still calls the plan public-spirited, so he keeps some pride in it. Discuss whether usefulness and honesty can really be separated as neatly as the father’s lesson suggests.
evidence: working with them diligently like so many emmets
though I pleaded the usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest

readings.title: London errata
readings.challenge: Keep track of each “erratum” Franklin names, and notice how quickly he moves from a confession to the next piece of news.
readings.focus: An eighteen-year-old on his own in London finds books, clever company and money trouble, and the older Franklin reckons up his mistakes.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. In 1724, at eighteen, Franklin sailed to London on the governor of Pennsylvania’s promise of letters of credit that never came, and found himself stranded there. His friend James Ralph came too, leaving a wife and child in Philadelphia. Before leaving, Franklin had an understanding with Deborah Read, his landlady’s daughter. An erratum, in printing, is a mistake listed for correction; a pistole is a gold coin; the Spectator was a famous London periodical of essays; a hackney writer copies documents for hire. Bernard Mandeville’s Fable of the Bees argued that private vices produce public benefits; Sir Hans Sloane was a physician and collector.
readings.contentNote: Franklin admits making unwanted advances to a woman who depended on him for loans; she refused him. He also describes neglecting his promise to Deborah Read.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to London, from lodgings with Ralph in Little Britain to the move to Watts’s printing-house; opens “Ralph and I were inseparable companions. We took lodgings together in Little Britain at…”; closes “…a still greater printing-house. Here I continued all the rest of my stay in London.”.

questions.prompt: Find each mistake Franklin calls an “erratum” in this passage. What do they have in common, and does the printer’s word suit all of them?
facilitatorNotes: Forgetting his engagement to Miss Read, printing his pamphlet on liberty and necessity, and his advances to Mrs. T——. An erratum is a misprint corrected at the back of a book, so the word presents a life as a text that can be revised.
The three are very different in seriousness, and some readers feel the neat word shrinks the last one. Others think Franklin is unusually frank to confess them at all.
evidence: This was another of the great errata of my life, which I should wish to correct if I were to live it over again.
My printing this pamphlet was another erratum.
I attempted familiarities (another erratum)

questions.prompt: How does Franklin describe Ralph’s search for work and his move to a country school? What does his taking the name “Mr. Franklin” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Ralph tries acting, a weekly paper and copying, then a school he thinks “below him.” Ashamed to be known as a schoolmaster, he borrows Franklin’s name; Franklin’s “did me the honour to assume mine” is dry irony.
Ralph is a foil: proud, hopeful of literary fame, and always borrowing. Ask whether the portrait is fair, since Franklin is also the man Ralph owes money to.
evidence: This, however, he deemed a business below him
he changed his name, and did me the honour to assume mine

questions.prompt: London offers Franklin books and famous men. Which opportunities does he take, and which slip away? What do they show about how a young printer could rise?
facilitatorNotes: He borrows from Wilcox’s huge stock of second-hand books, meets Mandeville through his pamphlet, and sells his asbestos purse to Sir Hans Sloane; he never gets to meet Newton. Ideas and curiosities open doors that his rank would not.
Readers who know the later chapters may connect Wilcox’s lending with Franklin’s subscription library in Philadelphia.
evidence: I might take, read, and return any of his books
who promis'd to give me an opportunity, sometime or other, of seeing Sir Isaac Newton, of which I was extreamly desirous; but this never happened

questions.prompt: Reread the account of Mrs. T——. How does Franklin judge his own conduct, and how does he describe the end of the friendship? Is his account fair to her and to Ralph?
facilitatorNotes: He admits he was “presuming upon my importance to her”: she needed his loans, and he used that. He calls her refusal “a proper resentment.” Then he turns at once to money and says losing Ralph’s friendship “relieved” him of a burden.
Some readers find the confession honest and brief; others notice that the sentences after it are about his own advantage. Ask what the speed of the turn suggests.
evidence: presuming upon my importance to her, I attempted familiarities (another erratum) which she repuls'd with a proper resentment
in the loss of his friendship I found myself relieved from a burthen

readings.title: Paper money, a rival’s fall and a marriage
readings.challenge: Track how each of Franklin’s gains depends on what other people think of him, and notice what he says plainly and what he passes over quickly.
readings.focus: A young printer builds credit, reputation and a household, and reckons his marriage as the correction of an earlier fault.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. This is the end of the part he wrote in 1771 as a letter to his son. Around 1729–1730, in his early twenties, Franklin owned a printing house in Philadelphia, still in debt for it. The Junto was his club of young tradesmen for discussion and self-improvement. Keimer was his former employer, and Bradford an older printer who also ran the post office. Deborah Read, whom he had courted before going to London, had in his absence married a man named Rogers, who left her and was rumoured to have another wife in England. Paper money was “sunk” when it was withdrawn; “blanks” are printed forms; a scrivener draws up legal documents.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Business Success and First Public Service, from the paper-money pamphlet to the memorandum that closes the first part; opens “ABOUT this time there was a cry among the people for more paper money, only fifteen…”; closes “…intended for the public. The affairs of the Revolution occasion'd the interruption.”.

questions.prompt: How did Franklin’s pamphlet on paper money help him twice over? What does the passage suggest about the link between public argument and private gain?
facilitatorNotes: It helped carry the vote for more currency, and his friends in the House rewarded him with the profitable job of printing the money. He sums up: “This was another advantage gain'd by my being able to write.”
Franklin does not hide the profit; he presents public service and business as naturally connected. Students may admire the candour or question the arrangement.
evidence: My friends there, who conceiv'd I had been of some service, thought fit to reward me by employing me in printing the money; a very profitable jobb and a great help to me.
This was another advantage gain'd by my being able to write.

questions.prompt: Franklin took care “not only to be in reality industrious and frugal, but to avoid all appearances to the contrary.” What does he do to manage appearances, and is this honest?
facilitatorNotes: He dresses plainly, avoids “idle diversion,” and wheels his paper home through the streets so that people see him working. His credit with merchants follows from that reputation.

Some readers call it calculated display; others note that he insists the industry was real and only the advertising was deliberate. His admission that a book sometimes “debauch'd” him from work is a small joke against the image.
evidence: I drest plainly; I was seen at no places of idle diversion.
I sometimes brought home the paper I purchas'd at the stores thro' the streets on a wheelbarrow

questions.prompt: Compare Franklin’s account of his rivals, Keimer, David Harry and Bradford, with his account of himself. What pattern does he want the reader to see?
facilitatorNotes: Harry is proud, dresses like a gentleman, lives expensively and neglects business, and fails; Keimer fails too; Bradford is “rich and easy” and blocks Franklin’s papers from the post riders. Franklin presents himself as the opposite in every case and promises never to imitate Bradford’s unkindness.
The pattern is a lesson in conduct, but it is also self-praise. Ask how Harry might have told the story of the partnership he “rejected with scorn.”
evidence: He was very proud, dress'd like a gentleman, liv'd expensively, took much diversion and pleasure abroad, ran in debt, and neglected his business
when I afterward came into his situation, I took care never to imitate it

questions.prompt: In the Godfrey courtship Franklin asks for money with the bride; with Deborah Read he takes on risks instead. What does he mean by calling the marriage the correction of “that great erratum,” and what does “as well as I could” admit?
facilitatorNotes: He asked the Godfreys for enough to pay his debt, and the match ended. Deborah’s first husband might still be alive and had left debts, yet they married in 1730. The erratum is his neglect of her while he was in London; marrying her repairs it only partly, which “as well as I could” concedes.
Modern readers may be struck by how businesslike the account is, and by how little we hear of Deborah’s own feelings. Franklin does say they “throve together” and tried “to make each other happy.”
evidence: I let her know that I expected as much money with their daughter as would pay off my remaining debt for the printing-house
Thus I corrected that great erratum as well as I could.

readings.title: Begun again at Passy: the library, a china bowl and a sermon
readings.challenge: Notice how Franklin, writing thirteen years after the first part and without it in hand, rebuilds his story, and test his advice against what he actually did.
readings.focus: Franklin turns his own habits, a subscription library, strategic modesty and a practical religion, into lessons for public readers.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. The first part, addressed to his son, ends with the founding of a subscription library in Philadelphia around 1730. Franklin took up the story again in 1784 at Passy, near Paris, where he was serving as the American minister to France; friends had written urging him to continue (their letters are not part of this text), and he did not have the first part with him. A conveyancer or scrivener draws up legal documents; a porringer is a small bowl; “plate” means silver tableware; a “mite” is a small gift. The Bible verse quoted is from Paul’s letter to the Philippians.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Business Success and First Public Service, from the continuation begun at Passy in 1784 to the end of the chapter; opens “[Continuation of the Account of my Life, begun at Passy, near Paris, 1784.]”; closes “…excuse it; my present purpose being to relate facts, and not to make apologies for them.”.

questions.prompt: How does Franklin begin again after thirteen years? What does he admit about his memory and his papers, and how should that affect our trust in what follows?
facilitatorNotes: He writes away from home “among my papers,” cannot check dates, and does not know whether he already told the library story, so he offers an account that “may be struck out.” In fact the first part had ended with that story, so readers can compare the two.

Admitting the limits makes him more trustworthy, not less, and the two versions agree on the key facts: fifty subscribers paying forty shillings each. His proud aside about standing before five kings shows the distance he has travelled since.
evidence: It might, too, be much better done if I were at home among my papers, which would aid my memory, and help to ascertain dates
which may be struck out if found to have been already given

questions.prompt: Franklin learned to present the library as “a scheme of a number of friends.” Why did that work, and is his advice about vanity humble or clever?
facilitatorNotes: People resisted a project that might raise one neighbour above the others, so he hid his own role and the subscriptions went “more smoothly.” He claims that someone vainer will try to take the credit and envy will then restore it to the real owner.
The advice is both: a small “sacrifice of your vanity” that is “amply repaid.” Notice that Franklin now claims the credit in print, which some students will find funny.
evidence: I therefore put myself as much as I could out of sight
The present little sacrifice of your vanity will afterwards be amply repaid.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the china bowl. What does “mark how luxury will enter families” mean, and what is Franklin’s tone toward his wife?
facilitatorNotes: Deborah bought a china bowl and silver spoon for twenty-three shillings because her husband “deserv'd” them as much as the neighbours; from there the family’s china and silver grew to several hundred pounds’ worth. The mock-solemn warning is a joke at his own principles.
Readers differ on the tone: affectionate teasing, or a husband treating his wife as the weak point in his thrift. He also praises her as a partner who folded pamphlets and tended shop.
evidence: But mark how luxury will enter families, and make a progress, in spite of principle
she thought her husband deserv'd a silver spoon and China bowl as well as any of his neighbors

questions.prompt: Why does Franklin stop going to hear the Presbyterian minister? What did he expect from the text from Philippians, and what does this show about what he thinks religion is for?
facilitatorNotes: He expected moral teaching from a verse about whatever is “true, honest, just, pure, lovely”; he got five duties to the church. He judged that the sermons aimed “rather to make us Presbyterians than good citizens,” since he held that the best service of God is “doing good to man.”
His last sentence refuses to apologize: his purpose is “to relate facts.” Students can debate whether that is honesty or a way of avoiding judgment.
evidence: their aim seeming to be rather to make us Presbyterians than good citizens
the most acceptable service of God was the doing good to man
my present purpose being to relate facts, and not to make apologies for them

readings.title: A plan for moral perfection
readings.challenge: Read the thirteen precepts slowly and decide which govern conduct and which govern thought. Then treat the little ruled book and the daily schedule as tools of a method.
readings.focus: Virtue treated as habit, trained by design and by keeping a record.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. He wrote this part at Passy, near Paris, in 1784, while serving as the American minister to France, recalling a project from his years as a young Philadelphia printer around 1730. “Elevation” here means tipsiness; venery is sexual activity. Pythagoras’s Golden Verses are ancient moral maxims. The mottoes come from Joseph Addison’s play Cato, the Roman orator Cicero (his Latin praises philosophy as the guide of life, which seeks out virtues and drives out vices), the Book of Proverbs, and the poet James Thomson.
readings.contentNote: The precept for Chastity refers briefly and frankly to sexual conduct.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter IX, from the start through his scheme of employment for the day; opens “IT was about this time I conceived the bold and arduous project of arriving at moral…”; closes “Night 10 Sleep. 11 12 1 2 3 4”.

questions.prompt: Why did Franklin’s first attempt to be faultless fail? What did he conclude about knowing what is right?
facilitatorNotes: While guarding against one fault he was surprised by another; “habit took the advantage of inattention.” He concluded that conviction alone does not prevent slipping: bad habits must be broken and good ones built.
Some readers find the insight obvious; others think its consequence, a practical method, is the original part. Both can be argued.
evidence: habit took the advantage of inattention; inclination was sometimes too strong for reason
the mere speculative conviction that it was our interest to be completely virtuous, was not sufficient to prevent our slipping

questions.prompt: Choose two of the thirteen precepts and restate them in your own words. Does Franklin’s wording make it easier or harder to tell each day whether you kept them?
facilitatorNotes: He chose “more names, with fewer ideas annex’d to each,” so most precepts are concrete enough to check nightly: “Eat not to dullness” sets a test, while “Imitate Jesus and Socrates” is open-ended.

Readers may notice that the list mixes outward conduct (Order, Frugality) with inner states (Tranquillity, or Sincerity’s “think innocently”). Strong answers connect wording to the black spots in the book.
evidence: to use rather more names, with fewer ideas annex'd to each, than a few names with more ideas
Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.

questions.prompt: How is the order of the virtues part of the plan? Explain one link in his chain and say whether you find it persuasive.
facilitatorNotes: Temperance gives a clear head; Silence helps him learn by listening and break a habit of “prattling, punning, and joking”; Order frees time; Resolution sustains the rest; Frugality and Industry free him from debt, which makes Sincerity and Justice easier.
Some readers question the economic link, that honesty comes easier with money; others find it realistic about the pressures of debt.
evidence: as the previous acquisition of some might facilitate the acquisition of certain others, I arrang'd them with that view
Frugality and Industry freeing me from my remaining debt, and producing affluence and independence, would make more easy the practice of Sincerity and Justice

readings.title: The speckled ax, and the trouble with pride
readings.challenge: Weigh what Franklin says the project achieved against what he admits it did not, and notice how his humour handles failure.
readings.focus: Partial success, the appearance and the reality of a virtue, and the persistence of pride.
readings.context: Recap: As a young printer Franklin set out to “arrive at moral perfection” by practising thirteen virtues, one each week, and marking each day’s faults with black spots in a little ruled book. A journeyman printer works for wages; a master runs his own shop. Foppery is fussy vanity. The Junto was a club of young Philadelphia tradesmen that Franklin founded for discussion. A Quaker is a member of the Religious Society of Friends.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter IX, from his use of the method through his remarks on humility and the note “Thus far written at Passy, 1784”; opens “I enter'd upon the execution of this plan for self-examination, and continu'd it with…”; closes “[Thus far written at Passy, 1784.]”.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the speckled ax. What arguments for giving up does “something, that pretended to be reason” suggest to Franklin?
facilitatorNotes: The neighbour tired of turning the grindstone and decided he liked “a speckled ax best.” The pretended reason said that strict perfection might be “foppery in morals,” would invite envy, and that a kind man should keep a few faults to make his friends comfortable.
The excuses are witty and partly true, which is why they tempt; Franklin calls them reason only in pretence. Students may decide whether any of them is actually sound.
evidence: but I think I like a speckled ax best
a benevolent man should allow a few faults in himself, to keep his friends in countenance

questions.prompt: Franklin says he never reached perfection but became “a better and a happier man” for trying. How does the comparison with copying engraved handwriting support this?
facilitatorNotes: Learners who copy a perfect model never match it, but their hand is improved by the effort; the ideal works as a direction rather than a finish line.
Readers can test this against the rewards he lists for his descendants (health, fortune, reputation, his country’s confidence), which some find complacent and others candid.
evidence: yet I was, by the endeavour, a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been if I had not attempted it
their hand is mended by the endeavour

questions.prompt: Franklin planned to argue that “vicious actions are not hurtful because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are hurtful.” What is the difference, and why would it suit a book meant for “people in all religions”?
facilitatorNotes: If harm is the reason, morality can be argued from human nature and self-interest without appealing to any one church’s authority, which fits his deliberate avoidance of sectarian doctrines.
Some readers welcome a practical, inclusive ethic; others worry that grounding virtue in interest, even in making “a poor man’s fortune,” turns goodness into a business strategy.
evidence: vicious actions are not hurtful because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are hurtful
no qualities were so likely to make a poor man's fortune as those of probity and integrity

questions.prompt: Franklin admits more success with the appearance of humility than with its reality. Is the habit he describes honest modesty or a persuasive technique? How does his final sentence on pride complicate your answer?
facilitatorNotes: He banned words such as “certainly” and began replies by granting cases where the other person was right; his views met “less contradiction,” and he credits the habit for his influence despite being “a bad speaker.” It is at least partly strategy.
The closing joke, that he would “probably be proud of my humility,” concedes the limits of self-mastery and wins the reader’s sympathy. Accept arguments for modesty, technique, or both.
evidence: I cannot boast of much success in acquiring the reality of this virtue, but I had a good deal with regard to the appearance of it.
I should probably be proud of my humility

readings.title: A United Party for Virtue
readings.challenge: Read the 1731 “Observations” as an argument in numbered steps. Then compare the proposed creed and secret society with the scheme of virtues that came before.
readings.focus: A young man’s theory of politics as competing interests, and his plan for an organized remedy.
readings.context: Recap: Franklin described his thirteen-week method of practising the virtues, admitted that he never mastered Order or overcame pride, and mentioned a “great and extensive project” he never completed. Here he resumes writing in Philadelphia in 1788, after the Revolution, and explains that project from a note he made in 1731, aged twenty-five. A sect is a religious group; the “professors” of a religion are those who profess it; “ingenuous” means candid and open.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter IX, from Franklin’s note on resuming at home in 1788 to the end of the chapter; opens “["I am now about to write at home, August, 1788, but cannot have the help expected from…”; closes “…divert his attention, makes the execution of that same plan his sole study and business.”.

questions.prompt: Summarize the 1731 “Observations” in two sentences. What does the young Franklin think drives “the great affairs of the world”?
facilitatorNotes: Parties pursue what they take to be their general interest; once they win, members turn to private interests and split, causing more confusion. Few act for their country’s good, and fewer for mankind’s, even when their actions do some good.
It is a realistic, almost cynical account from someone who would spend his life in parties and public business. Students may test it against politics they know.
evidence: That the great affairs of the world, the wars, revolutions, etc., are carried on and effected by parties.
That fewer still, in public affairs, act with a view to the good of mankind.

questions.prompt: Franklin says his creed contains “the essentials of every known religion.” What does it include, and what does it leave out?
facilitatorNotes: One God, providence, worship, an immortal soul, reward and punishment, and above all “doing good to man.” It leaves out the doctrines and practices that divide churches.
Some readers see an inclusive common ground; others see a creed so thin that it mainly serves his practical aims. Both readings are defensible from the list.
evidence: But that the most acceptable service of God is doing good to man.
containing, as I thought, the essentials of every known religion

questions.prompt: Why should the Society of the Free and Easy be secret and begin among “young and single men only”? What does its name promise, and what does the final sentence reveal about Franklin’s view of himself?
facilitatorNotes: Secrecy keeps out “improper persons,” and members would advance one another’s business: part moral club, part network. “Free” means free from vice and from debt, which he calls “a species of slavery to his creditors.”
The last sentence, that one able man with a good plan and single focus “may work great changes,” reads like a summary of his own career. Readers may also notice whom the society excludes.
evidence: free from debt, which exposes a man to confinement, and a species of slavery to his creditors
one man of tolerable abilities may work great changes, and accomplish great affairs among mankind

readings.title: A brother’s son, secret clubs and a borrowed book
readings.challenge: Franklin turns almost every event into a lesson for the reader. Separate each event from the lesson he draws, and test whether the lesson follows.
readings.focus: Family repair, a hard-won lesson about smallpox, and Franklin’s methods for gaining influence: secret networks, a borrowed book and careful accounts.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. In the 1730s Franklin, now in his thirties, ran a successful printing house and newspaper in Philadelphia. As a teenager he had run away from his apprenticeship to his older brother James, a Boston printer. The Junto was Franklin’s club of tradesmen who debated questions (“queries”) for mutual improvement. Smallpox inoculation meant deliberately giving someone a mild case through a small cut; it usually protected against the deadly natural disease but carried some risk. The General Assembly was Pennsylvania’s elected legislature; Bradford, his “old competitor,” was the printer who had also run the post office.
readings.contentNote: Franklin briefly recalls the death of his four-year-old son from smallpox.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard’s Almanac and Other Activities, from the visit to Boston through the post office; opens “After ten years' absence from Boston, and having become easy in my circumstances, I made…”; closes “…is the most powerful of all recommendations to new employments and increase of business.”.

questions.prompt: Two family events open the passage. How does Franklin present each as making up for, or learning from, a mistake?
facilitatorNotes: He takes in his dying brother’s son and later gives him new types, “ample amends” for having left his apprenticeship to that brother. His son’s death from smallpox becomes advice: parents who fear inoculation should know “the regret may be the same either way.”
Ask how it feels to read a child’s death turned into a public argument in two sentences. Some readers find it cold; others see grief that he “still” feels being put to use.
evidence: Thus it was that I made my brother ample amends for the service I had depriv'd him of by leaving him so early.
I long regretted bitterly, and still regret that I had not given it to him by inoculation.
the regret may be the same either way, and that, therefore, the safer should be chosen

questions.prompt: The Junto’s members each formed a “subordinate club” without telling its members about the connection. What advantages does Franklin list, and how do you judge the secrecy?
facilitatorNotes: Improving more young citizens, learning what people thought, helping members’ business, and spreading the Junto’s views to influence public opinion. The new clubs did not know they were being used for that last purpose.
Some readers see an early civic network; others see quiet manipulation. Franklin seems untroubled and even promises “instances” of how well it worked.
evidence: without informing them of the connection with the Junto
our power of doing good by spreading thro' the several clubs the sentiments of the Junto
our views of influencing the public opinion on particular occasions

questions.prompt: Explain the borrowed-book strategy. Why might asking a favour win over an opponent better than doing him one?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of flattering the new member, Franklin asked to borrow a rare book and thanked him warmly; the man became a friend for life. Having helped Franklin once, he had a reason to think well of him, as the maxim says.
Students may notice that the request also flattered the man’s taste and learning. Ask whether the method is sincere friendship or skilful management, or both.
evidence: He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged.
I did not, however, aim at gaining his favour by paying any servile respect to him

questions.prompt: Franklin explains what he gained as clerk and as postmaster, then offers lessons to “young men.” How does he mix self-interest and advice, and does his conduct toward Bradford show the virtue he claims?
facilitatorNotes: He openly values the clerkship for the printing jobs it secured and the post office for his newspaper. Bradford lost the post office through careless accounts; Franklin says he did not retaliate by barring Bradford’s papers, as Bradford had once barred his.
He still enjoys reporting that his rival’s paper “declin'd proportionately.” Readers can decide whether the restraint is generosity, prudence, or both.
evidence: which secur'd to me the business of printing the votes, laws, paper money, and other occasional jobbs for the public, that, on the whole, were very profitable
I was satisfy'd without retaliating his refusal
Thus he suffer'd greatly from his neglect in due accounting

readings.title: The city watch and the Union Fire Company
readings.challenge: Notice how Franklin turns a complaint into a proposal and a proposal into an institution. Track each step.
readings.focus: Civic improvement by a club of tradesmen: a fairer tax, and a volunteer fire company that outlived its founders.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. He wrote this part in Philadelphia in 1788, looking back to the 1730s. The Junto was the club of young tradesmen he had founded in 1727 to discuss ideas and improve themselves. The city was divided into wards, each with a constable who organised the night watch from local householders (“housekeepers”). Six shillings was a modest sum, fifty pounds a small estate; “tippling” is drinking; conflagrations are large fires.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter XI, from the start through the history of the Union Fire Company; opens “I BEGAN now to turn my thoughts a little to public affairs, beginning, however, with…”; closes “…have often been extinguished before the house in which they began has been half consumed.”.

questions.prompt: Franklin finds two faults with the city watch. What are they, and which does he stress “more particularly”?
facilitatorNotes: The watch was badly kept, with drinking “ragamuffins” and neglected rounds, and it was paid for unfairly: a poor widow paid the same six shillings as the richest merchant. He stresses the unfairness, proposing paid watchmen and a tax “proportion’d to the property.”
Students may connect this with modern arguments over flat and proportional taxes. Franklin’s argument rests on what each person has to protect.
evidence: insisting more particularly on the inequality of this six-shilling tax
the levying a tax that should be proportion'd to the property

questions.prompt: The plan was passed to the other clubs “as arising in each of them.” Why might Franklin hide his authorship, and why does he count the plan a success though it was not adopted at once?
facilitatorNotes: If each club believed the idea its own, members would support it without envy of its author. And though no law passed immediately, the plan prepared “the minds of people,” so that the change came easily years later.
Some readers admire this patient, self-effacing method; others find it a little calculating. Either way, Franklin is telling how change happens slowly.
evidence: was communicated to the other clubs, but as arising in each of them
by preparing the minds of people for the change, it paved the way for the law obtained a few years after

questions.prompt: How did the fire company work, and what made it last more than fifty years?
facilitatorNotes: Members kept buckets, bags and baskets ready, came to every fire, and met monthly for “a social evening.” Fines for missing meetings bought fire-engines and ladders, so even absence improved the equipment, and new companies formed as more people wanted to join.
Franklin’s pride shows: “I question whether there is a city in the world better provided.” Students may weigh that boast against his evidence about houses lost to fire.
evidence: we agreed to meet once a month and spend a social evening together
The small fines that have been paid by members for absence at the monthly meetings have been apply'd to the purchase of fire-engines
I question whether there is a city in the world better provided

readings.title: Franklin and the preacher Whitefield
readings.challenge: Watch Franklin observing Whitefield: as a listener, a friend and a scientist. Find one moment when he laughs at himself.
readings.focus: A sceptic’s portrait of a great preacher, full of affection, comedy and measurement.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. He wrote this part in Philadelphia in 1788. George Whitefield (1714–1770), an English preacher, toured the colonies drawing enormous outdoor crowds; his preaching fed the religious revival later called the Great Awakening. “Itinerant” means travelling; Georgia had been founded in 1733. Pistoles were Spanish gold coins; Westminster Hall is a great medieval hall in London; the Mufti of Constantinople was the chief Islamic scholar of the Ottoman Empire. Quakers addressed one another as “Friend” and used “thee.” Litera scripta manet is Latin for “the written word remains”; votaries and proselytes are devoted followers and converts.
readings.contentNote: Franklin uses “Mohammedanism,” an old term for Islam that many Muslims find offensive.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter XI, the passage on George Whitefield; opens “In 1739 arrived among us from Ireland the Reverend Mr. Whitefield, who had made himself…”; closes “…variety of excellences as their enthusiastic admiration might wish him to have possessed.”.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the collection for the Orphan House. How does Franklin make it comic, and what does it prove?
facilitatorNotes: He resolves to give nothing, then moves from copper to silver to gold as the sermon goes on, and ends by emptying his pocket. The escalation, told in his own deadpan voice, shows Whitefield’s power over “hearts and purses,” with Franklin himself as the evidence.
The second story doubles the joke: a friend who emptied his pockets in advance tries to borrow money, and a Quaker neighbour refuses because he “seems to be out of thy right senses.”
evidence: I silently resolved he should get nothing from me.
I empty'd my pocket wholly into the collector's dish, gold and all.
for thee seems to be out of thy right senses.

questions.prompt: Describe Franklin’s experiment on Whitefield’s voice. What does it show about how Franklin thinks?
facilitatorNotes: He walked backward down Market Street until the voice faded, imagined a half-circle with that distance as its radius, allowed two square feet per listener, and calculated that more than thirty thousand people could hear. The result made him believe newspaper reports of huge crowds and ancient stories of generals addressing armies.
Even at a revival he measures and tests. His remark that rehearsed sermons please like “an excellent piece of musick” shows the same habit of analysing his own pleasure.
evidence: Imagining then a semicircle, of which my distance should be the radius
I computed that he might well be heard by more than thirty thousand.
a pleasure of much the same kind with that receiv'd from an excellent piece of musick

questions.prompt: Franklin calls theirs “a mere civil friendship.” How does the “for Christ’s sake” exchange show its terms, and what does Franklin think of Whitefield’s writing?
facilitatorNotes: Whitefield thanks him in religious terms; Franklin insists the offer was “for your sake,” personal friendship rather than piety, and a friend jokes that he kept the debt “on earth.” Franklin also vouches for Whitefield’s honesty, saying his word counts more because they shared no religion.

On writing, Franklin observes that printed sermons gave critics something fixed to attack; had Whitefield written nothing, followers could have imagined any virtues for him. Students may find the remark shrewd, cynical, or both.
evidence: it was not for Christ's sake, but for your sake.
my testimony in his favour ought to have the more weight, as we had no religious connection
his proselytes would be left at liberty to feign for him as great a variety of excellences

readings.title: Plain Truth and the Association
readings.challenge: List the steps Franklin takes to defend a colony that has no militia. For each, ask what made it work.
readings.focus: A private citizen organizes a volunteer army, a lottery and a borrowed battery, and deals carefully with a pacifist legislature.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. In the 1740s Britain was at war with Spain and then France, and enemy privateers threatened Philadelphia from the sea. Pennsylvania had no militia, because its Assembly was controlled by Quakers, members of a Christian group whose principles forbid war. The proprietaries were the Penn family, who owned the colony. Franklin had been clerk of the Assembly since 1736. A battery is a set of cannon in a fortification; merlons are the solid parts of its wall between the gun openings; a bumper is a full glass. The Philosophical Society he mentions became the American Philosophical Society.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Defense of the Province, from the plan for an academy to the Quakers’ view of defensive war; opens “I HAD, on the whole, abundant reason to be satisfied with my being established in…”; closes “…Quakers, in favour of defense, which I believe convinc'd most of their younger people.”.

questions.prompt: How did Franklin turn his pamphlet Plain Truth into an army? What preparations at the meeting help explain the result?
facilitatorNotes: He promised an association in the pamphlet, then held a meeting with printed copies ready and “pens and ink dispers'd all over the room,” explained it briefly, and let people sign at once. Twelve hundred signed that night and over ten thousand in the end.
Franklin knew how to make agreement easy. Students can compare this with how petitions and sign-ups work today.
evidence: I had prepared a number of printed copies, and provided pens and ink dispers'd all over the room.
the subscribers amounted at length to upward of ten thousand

questions.prompt: Franklin declines to be colonel but takes his turn on guard “as a common soldier.” Why might he describe both choices, and what does the cannon story at Governor Clinton’s dinner add?
facilitatorNotes: He presents himself as an organizer without personal ambition, which fits his rule of keeping out of sight to win cooperation. The Madeira story, six cannon becoming ten and then eighteen as the glasses empty, shows the comic side of getting things done.
Some readers will see modesty; others will see a carefully managed image. Both are supported by what he chooses to tell.
evidence: chose me for their colonel; but, conceiving myself unfit, I declin'd that station
After a few more bumpers he advanc'd to ten; and at length he very good-naturedly conceded eighteen.
I regularly took my turn of duty there as a common soldier

questions.prompt: Franklin, who seldom went to church, proposes a public fast “Calling in the aid of religion.” What was the fast for? Is this sincere, practical, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted to “implore the blessing of Heaven,” but he also notes the result: the clergy of every sect could urge their congregations to join the association. His New England upbringing supplied the form of the proclamation.
The phrase “Calling in the aid of religion” makes religion sound like an ally to recruit. Students can weigh it against his stated beliefs about doing good.
evidence: Calling in the aid of religion, I propos'd to them the proclaiming a fast
This gave the clergy of the different sects an opportunity of influencing their congregations to join in the association

questions.prompt: Explain Franklin’s rule about offices: “never ask, never refuse, nor ever resign.” What does his last remark about the Quakers suggest about how he reads people?
facilitatorNotes: He would not resign under pressure, because resigning would surrender “my right of some time or other making reprisals.” He judges that the Quakers did not mind defence as long as they did not have to take part: many were against offensive war but not defensive.
The tone is dry rather than contemptuous. Ask whether he is fair to people trying to keep a religious principle in a dangerous time.
evidence: I shall never ask, never refuse, nor ever resign an office.
the defense of the country was not disagreeable to any of them, provided they were not requir'd to assist in it

readings.title: The fire company vote and “other grain”
readings.challenge: Follow the fire-company meeting minute by minute, then collect every way in which Quakers found to support defence without saying so.
readings.focus: Franklin’s amused, respectful account of how a pacifist people handled the demands of war.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. In the late 1740s Franklin organized a volunteer association to defend Philadelphia and proposed a lottery to pay for a battery of cannon. Pennsylvania’s Assembly was controlled by Quakers (who call themselves Friends), whose principles forbid war. The Union Fire Company was a volunteer firefighting club Franklin had founded. William Penn, a Quaker, founded Pennsylvania; James Logan came over as his secretary. Louisburg was a French fortress on Cape Breton Island captured by New England troops in 1745. A fire-engine was a hand pump on wheels; a “great gun” is a cannon.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Defense of the Province, from the vote in the fire company to the joke about a fire-engine; opens “A transaction in our fire company gave me some insight into their prevailing sentiments.…”; closes “…Assembly; your equivocal project would be just a match for their wheat or other grain."”.

questions.prompt: How did Franklin win the fire-company vote? Why did he agree to wait “another hour” after “a little seeming hesitation”?
facilitatorNotes: Eight Quaker members waiting at a nearby tavern promised to vote with him if needed but hoped not to be called. Knowing he had a majority, he could appear generous by granting the delay; no opponents came, and the resolution passed eight to one.
The “seeming hesitation” is a small performance. Franklin then turns the vote into evidence: he estimates that only one Quaker in twenty-one sincerely opposed defence.
evidence: Being thus secure of a majority, I went up, and after a little seeming hesitation, agreed to a delay of another hour.
I afterward estimated the proportion of Quakers sincerely against defense as one to twenty-one only

questions.prompt: What does James Logan’s answer to William Penn reveal? Why might Franklin include this story?
facilitatorNotes: Penn rebuked Logan for staying on deck to help fight, but Logan points out that Penn did not order him below while danger seemed real. The retort exposes how a principle can be kept by letting others do the fighting.
Logan was himself a Quaker who supported defence, so the story supports Franklin’s case from inside the sect. Students may find it unfair to Penn, who did, after all, go below.
evidence: I being thy servant, why did thee not order me to come down?
But thee was willing enough that I should stay and help to fight the ship when thee thought there was danger.

questions.prompt: Explain “for the king’s use” and “other grain is gunpowder.” Are these evasions hypocrisy, or a reasonable compromise?
facilitatorNotes: The Assembly granted war money without naming its purpose, and voted funds for “bread, flour, wheat or other grain” so the governor could buy gunpowder. They kept their principle in words while meeting the demand in fact.

Some readers see hypocrisy; others see a practical way to live with both conscience and duty. Franklin’s own joke about buying a “great gun” as a “fire-engine” shows he enjoys the trick, and his friend Syng teases him for learning it from the Assembly.
evidence: The common mode at last was, to grant money under the phrase of its being "for the king's use," and never to inquire how it was applied.
I shall take the money, for I understand very well their meaning; other grain is gunpowder
we will buy a great gun, which is certainly a fire-engine

readings.title: The Albany Plan and the proprietary governors
readings.challenge: Follow two stories of colonial government: a plan that failed and a quarrel that was solved by a trick of finance. Ask what Franklin wants the reader to conclude about each.
readings.focus: A plan of union rejected from both sides, the manners of political enemies, and the money behind the quarrels.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. He wrote this part in 1788. In 1754, with war against France and its Native allies expected, commissioners from several colonies met at Albany, New York, with chiefs of the Six Nations (the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy). The Lords of Trade oversaw the colonies from London; “prerogative” is the crown’s power. Pennsylvania was a proprietary colony: the Penn family owned it and appointed its governors, who followed their instructions, while the elected Assembly, long led by Quakers, voted taxes. The couplet is from John Dryden’s translation of the Roman poet Juvenal; Sancho Panza is the squire in Don Quixote; Crown Point was a French fort on Lake Champlain. The Loan Office lent paper money to colonists; an excise is a tax on goods.
readings.contentNote: At a dinner the governor and a friend joke about selling enslaved Black people, and Franklin replies with a pun on “blacken” and the racist word “negrofied.” Native nations are called “the Indians.”

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapters XIV and XV, complete; opens “IN 1754, war with France being again apprehended, a congress of commissioners from the…”; closes “…of his embassy, and ever after bore for me the most cordial and affectionate friendship.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the Albany Plan fail, and why does Franklin treat its double rejection as evidence that it was right?
facilitatorNotes: The colonial assemblies thought it gave too much power to the crown; in England it seemed “too much of the democratic.” Franklin concludes that opposite objections suggest “the true medium,” and that the plan would have made British troops and taxes unnecessary and so avoided “the bloody contest,” the Revolution.
Students may test the logic: a plan attacked from both sides is not necessarily right. Franklin is also writing in 1788, with hindsight.
evidence: the assemblies did not adopt it, as they all thought there was too much prerogative in it, and in England it was judg'd to have too much of the democratic
makes me suspect that it was really the true medium
the subsequent pretence for taxing America, and the bloody contest it occasioned, would have been avoided

questions.prompt: What does Franklin think of “disputing, contradicting, and confuting people”? How does his friendship with Governor Morris complicate the picture?
facilitatorNotes: Disputers “get victory sometimes, but they never get good will.” Morris loved argument and broke his promise to avoid disputes at once. Yet though their public messages were “indecently abusive,” the two men stayed friends and often dined together.
Students may compare this separation of public battle and private civility with politics today, and decide whether it is admirable or strange.
evidence: They get victory sometimes, but they never get good will, which would be of more use to them.
no personal difference between him and me was occasion'd by the contest, and we often din'd together

questions.prompt: At the governor’s dinner, how do the jokes work, and what do they reveal about the men at the table and their time?
facilitatorNotes: Morris jokes about Sancho Panza wanting to govern Black people so he could sell them; a guest suggests Franklin “sell” the Quakers. Franklin’s reply turns “blacken” (to smear a reputation) into a political point: the governor’s attacks have only blackened himself.

The wit wins the exchange, but every joke depends on treating enslaved people as goods for sale and Blackness as disgrace, and no one at the table objects. Franklin owned enslaved people in these years; late in life he became president of an abolition society. Students can discuss how a reader should hold both facts.
evidence: requested it might be a government of blacks, as then, if he could not agree with his people, he might sell them
has not yet blacked them enough.

questions.prompt: What, according to Franklin, lay “at bottom” of the quarrels? How did he get the aid to New England past the governor?
facilitatorNotes: The proprietors told their governors to pass no tax for defence “unless their vast estates” were exempted, which Franklin calls “incredible meanness.” He had the Assembly issue interest-bearing orders on the Loan Office, which people bought eagerly and used as money, so the provisions were paid for without the governor’s consent.
“Thus this important affair was by my means completed”: Franklin is never shy about his own part. Students may judge whether the scheme was clever, sly, or both.
evidence: unless their vast estates were in the same act expressly excused
I then suggested a method of doing the business without the governor
Thus this important affair was by my means completed.

readings.title: Braddock’s confidence and defeat
readings.challenge: Follow Franklin’s warning, the general’s reply and the ambush as one argument about judgment. Then notice where the narrator writing in 1788 shows through.
readings.focus: Overconfidence, the tact of a warning, and an early crack in colonial faith in British power.
readings.context: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) wrote his Autobiography in several stages between 1771 and his last years; this edition divides it into chapters. In 1755, early in the war between Britain and France for North America, the British general Edward Braddock marched against Fort Duquesne, a French fort where Pittsburgh now stands; Franklin, a Pennsylvania leader, had found wagons and horses for his army. Regulars are professional soldiers; militia are part-time local soldiers; an ambuscade is an ambush; Niagara and Frontenac were other French forts. Franklin wrote this section in 1788, after the Revolution.
readings.contentNote: Battle deaths are reported in numbers, and soldiers plunder settlers. Braddock calls Native warriors “savages,” a slur; Franklin’s “Indians” is the usual term of his time.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Chapter XVI, Braddock’s Expedition, from Franklin’s judgment of the general through Braddock’s last words; opens “This general was, I think, a brave man, and might probably have made a figure as a good…”; closes “…shall better know how to deal with them another time"; and dy'd in a few minutes after.”.

questions.prompt: What three faults does Franklin find in Braddock, and how does the general’s treatment of George Croghan’s hundred scouts illustrate them?
facilitatorNotes: Too much self-confidence, too high an opinion of regular troops, and too low an opinion of Americans and Indians. He “slighted and neglected” the Native scouts who could have guided him, and they left; then the fire from the woods was his “first intelligence” of the enemy.
Franklin also grants that Braddock was brave and might have done well “in some European war.” Ask why he opens with that concession.
evidence: too much self-confidence, too high an opinion of the validity of regular troops, and too mean a one of both Americans and Indians
which was the first intelligence the general had of an enemy's being near him

questions.prompt: Look at how Franklin voices his warning. Why does he begin “To be sure, sir,” and why does he stop after Braddock’s reply? Do you trust this account, written more than thirty years later?
facilitatorNotes: He flatters before cautioning, gives the vivid image of an army “cut like a thread,” then defers to “a military man in matters of his profession.” The scene makes him both prophet and model of tact, much like the humility he describes practising in Chapter IX.
Readers may accept it, or suspect that hindsight has polished the memory. The narrator knows the outcome while he tells the conversation.
evidence: to be cut like a thread into several pieces
I was conscious of an impropriety in my disputing with a military man in matters of his profession, and said no more

questions.prompt: What larger conclusion does Franklin draw from the defeat and the soldiers’ conduct on the march? How does his comparison with “our French friends in 1781” reveal when he was writing?
facilitatorNotes: The rout gave Americans “the first suspicion” that British regulars were overrated, and their plundering put colonists out of conceit of such defenders. Writing after the Revolution, he sets them beside the French allies who took not “a pig, a chicken, or even an apple.”

The memoir reads 1755 through the lens of independence. Braddock’s dying “Who would have thought it?” can serve as the epitaph of the overconfidence Franklin described, or as a moment of human surprise that invites some sympathy.
evidence: This whole transaction gave us Americans the first suspicion that our exalted ideas of the prowess of British regulars had not been well founded.
Who would have thought it?
